profile.what: Micron is one of three companies in the world that make DRAM memory at scale (with Samsung and SK Hynix), and a major maker of NAND flash storage. Its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) sits next to the processors in AI servers.
profile.money: Micron sells memory chips by the gigabyte to makers of servers, PCs, phones and cars. Memory is close to a commodity, so prices swing with supply and demand: in shortages margins are enormous, in gluts the company can lose money. HBM for AI has lifted prices and made the current upswing unusually strong.
profile.valued: Memory stocks are valued on price to book value and on mid-cycle earnings, not on peak earnings: a low P/E at the top of the cycle is a warning, not a bargain. The stock moves with memory prices and AI-server demand.

summary.sentence: A memory-chip maker in a powerful upcycle; memory cycles have always turned.
strengths: AI demand has pushed margins to record highs.
Very low debt after the upturn.
risks: Lost money as recently as fiscal 2023.

meaning.what_it_does: Makes memory chips (DRAM and NAND) used in data centres, phones and PCs.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Sells memory at market prices that swing with supply and demand.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: AI servers need far more memory, and only three companies make leading-edge DRAM.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Memory prices collapse when supply catches up, as they did in fiscal 2023.

moat.summary: An oligopoly, but memory is largely interchangeable, so price is set by the market.

industry.summary: Memory is both a commodity and a technology race: each generation must be matched or the business loses money.

management.summary: Has navigated brutal cycles and kept debt low.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $4.0B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 3.2x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 0–3% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 75%; cost of capital 10.7%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
